claim: Prioritizing memory for valuable information can promote adaptive behavior across the lifespan.
source: Prioritizing memory for valuable information can promote adaptive behavior across the lifespan, but it is unclear how the neurocognitive mechanisms that enable the selective acquisition of useful knowledge develop.
evidence: This is a general statement about memory function that draws from established scientific understanding.

claim: The ability to use learned value signals to selectively enhance memory for useful information strengthened throughout childhood and into adolescence.
source: We found that the ability to use learned value signals to selectively enhance memory for useful information strengthened throughout childhood and into adolescence.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study's behavioral results.

claim: Encoding and retrieval of high- vs. low-value information was associated with increased activation in striatal and prefrontal regions implicated in value processing and cognitive control.
source: Encoding and retrieval of high- vs. low-value information was associated with increased activation in striatal and prefrontal regions implicated in value processing and cognitive control.
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI data collected during the study.

claim: Age-related increases in value-based lateral prefrontal cortex modulation mediated the relation between age and memory selectivity.
source: Age-related increases in value-based lateral prefrontal cortex modulation mediated the relation between age and memory selectivity.
evidence: This claim is supported by mediation analysis of neuroimaging and behavioral data.

claim: Developmental increases in the strategic engagement of the prefrontal cortex support the emergence of adaptive memory.
source: Our findings demonstrate that developmental increases in the strategic engagement of the prefrontal cortex support the emergence of adaptive memory.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the study's data.

claim: By adulthood, individuals demonstrate the ability to prioritize memory for information that is likely to be most rewarding in the future.
source: By adulthood, individuals demonstrate the ability to prioritize memory for information that is likely to be most rewarding in the future (Adcock et al., 2006; Cohen et al., 2019b; Cohen et al., 2014; Hennessee et al., 2019; Shigemune et al., 2014; Shohamy and Adcock, 2010; Wittmann et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Children demonstrate weaker memory selectivity, often remembering relatively inconsequential information at the expense of higher value items or associations.
source: Children, however, demonstrate weaker memory selectivity, often remembering relatively inconsequential information at the expense of higher value items or associations (Castel et al., 2011; Hanten et al., 2007; Nussenbaum et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The use of value to guide encoding and retrieval processes emerges and strengthens gradually throughout childhood and adolescence.
source: Behavioral studies have found that the use of value to guide encoding and retrieval processes emerges and strengthens gradually throughout childhood and adolescence, promoting more efficient acquisition of useful knowledge with increasing age (Castel et al., 2011; Hanten et al., 2007; Nussenbaum et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior behavioral studies.

claim: No prior studies have investigated how the developing brain prioritizes memories based on their relative utility.
source: It is unclear, however, how changes in brain activity support this observed emergence of motivated memory. Although a large literature has examined developmental change in the neural mechanisms that support memory from early childhood to young adulthood (Ghetti and Fandakova, 2020; Ofen, 2012; Shing et al., 2010), no prior studies have investigated how the developing brain prioritizes memories based on their relative utility.
evidence: This claim is based on a review of existing literature and identifies a gap in the research.

claim: Prioritizing valuable information in memory requires both determining the value of information and strategically modulating encoding accordingly.
source: Prioritizing valuable information in memory requires both determining the value of information and strategically modulating encoding accordingly.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about the cognitive processes involved in motivated memory.

claim: In most adult studies of motivated memory, determining the value of information is trivial for participants because experimenters label to-be-remembered information with explicit value cues.
source: The vast majority of adult studies have focused only on the strategic use of value to guide memory — in most studies of motivated memory, determining the value of information is trivial for participants because experimenters label to-be-remembered information with explicit value cues (e.g. dollar signs, stars, point amounts) (Adcock et al., 2006; Castel et al., 2011; Cohen et al., 2014; Murty et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim characterizes the methodology of prior research studies.

claim: In real-world contexts, individuals must derive the value of information from the statistics of their environments.
source: However, in real-world contexts, individuals must derive the value of information from the statistics of their environments.
evidence: This is a general statement about real-world cognitive processes.

claim: Young adults can use naturalistic value signals to prioritize memory for useful information.
source: In a recent behavioral study (Nussenbaum et al., 2020), we demonstrated that young adults could use naturalistic value signals to prioritize memory for useful information.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior study by the authors.

claim: Across many environments, the frequency of encountering something in the past predicts the frequency of encountering it in the future.
source: Across many environments, the frequency of encountering something in the past predicts the frequency of encountering it in the future.
evidence: This is a general principle about environmental statistics.

claim: Frequency can signal information utility.
source: In this way, frequency can signal information utility (Anderson and Milson, 1989; Anderson and Schooler, 1991; Liu et al., 2021; Pachur et al., 2014; Rich and Gureckis, 2018; Stevens et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Individuals exploited naturalistic value signals and demonstrated better memory for information associated with high- relative to low-frequency items.
source: We found that individuals exploited these naturalistic value signals and demonstrated better memory for information associated with high- relative to low-frequency items.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior behavioral study by the authors.

claim: The strategic prioritization of high-value information in memory increased from age 7 to age 25.
source: Critically, this pattern of results varied with age; the strategic prioritization of high-value information in memory increased from age 7 to age 25 (Nussenbaum et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior study by the authors.

claim: Deriving value from the structure of the environment requires the learning of statistical regularities.
source: Deriving value from the structure of the environment first requires the learning of statistical regularities.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about cognitive processes.

claim: The parahippocampal cortex demonstrates reduced responsivity to repeated relative to novel presentations of items (i.e. 'repetition suppression').
source: Neurally, medial temporal lobe regions may support sensitivity to item repetitions. The parahippocampal cortex in particular demonstrates reduced responsivity to repeated relative to novel presentations of items (i.e. 'repetition suppression') (Gonsalves et al., 2005; Kirchhoff et al., 2000; Köhler et al., 2005; O'Kane et al., 2005; Turk-Browne et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior neuroimaging research.

claim: Repetition suppression has been shown to be sensitive to the statistical context of the environment, suggesting that suppression may reflect stimulus expectation and index learning of environmental regularities.
source: Although some accounts of repetition suppression suggest that attenuated responses simply indicate neural 'fatigue,' the phenomenon has also been shown to be sensitive to the statistical context of the environment, suggesting that suppression may reflect stimulus expectation and index learning of environmental regularities (Auksztulewicz and Friston, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Repetition suppression has been shown to relate to implicit memory for repeated items.
source: Repetition suppression has also been shown to relate to implicit memory for repeated items (Ward et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Children and adolescents demonstrate neural repetition suppression effects.
source: Paralleling their robust implicit learning abilities (Amso and Davidow, 2012; Finn et al., 2016; Meulemans et al., 1998), children and adolescents also demonstrate neural repetition suppression effects (Nordt et al., 2016; Scherf et al., 2011; Turi et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Repetition suppression may increase throughout childhood.
source: although repetition suppression — and the ability to learn the statistical structure of the environment — may increase throughout childhood (Scherf et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Frequency knowledge may be instantiated as value signals, engaging regions along the mesolimbic dopamine pathway that have been implicated in reward anticipation and the encoding of stimulus and action values.
source: When individuals need to remember information associated with previously encountered stimuli (e.g. the grocery store aisle where an ingredient is located), frequency knowledge may be instantiated as value signals, engaging regions along the mesolimbic dopamine pathway that have been implicated in reward anticipation and the encoding of stimulus and action values.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement based on prior knowledge of neural systems.

claim: Regions along the mesolimbic dopamine pathway include the ventral tegmental area (VTA) and the ventral and dorsal striatum.
source: These areas include the ventral tegmental area (VTA) and the ventral and dorsal striatum (Adcock et al., 2006; Liljeholm and O'Doherty, 2012; Shigemune et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Using learned value signals to guide memory likely requires cognitive control.
source: Using these learned value signals to guide memory likely requires cognitive control (Castel et al., 2007; Cohen et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Value responses in the striatum may signal the need for increased engagement of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC).
source: Value responses in the striatum may signal the need for increased engagement of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) (Botvinick and Braver, 2015), which supports the implementation of strategic control.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) supports the implementation of strategic control.
source: Value responses in the striatum may signal the need for increased engagement of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) (Botvinick and Braver, 2015), which supports the implementation of strategic control.
evidence: This is a statement about the function of the dlPFC based on established neuroscience knowledge.

claim: Enhanced recruitment of control processes promotes the use of deeper and more elaborative encoding strategies.
source: Enhanced recruitment of control processes promotes the use of deeper and more elaborative encoding strategies (Cohen et al., 2019b; Cohen et al., 2014; Miotto et al., 2006; Uncapher and Wagner, 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Enhanced recruitment of control processes promotes the selection and maintenance of effective retrieval and post-retrieval monitoring strategies.
source: as well as the selection and maintenance of effective retrieval and post-retrieval monitoring strategies (Libby and Lipe, 1992; Scimeca and Badre, 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The use of value to proactively upregulate cognitive control responses improves throughout development.
source: The use of value to proactively upregulate cognitive control responses improves throughout development, though the specific trajectory of improvement may relate to the control demands of a given task (Davidow et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Selectively enhancing the use of encoding and retrieval strategies requires tight coordination between subcortical regions involved in value processing and prefrontal areas implicated in control.
source: Selectively enhancing the use of encoding and retrieval strategies requires not only tight coordination between subcortical regions involved in value processing and prefrontal areas implicated in control (Murty and Adcock, 2014), but also an available repertoire of memory strategies to implement.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Children and adolescents demonstrate reduced use of strategic control in the absence of value cues.
source: Even in the absence of value cues, children and adolescents demonstrate reduced use of strategic control (Bjorkland et al., 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Children and adolescents demonstrate reduced lateral prefrontal engagement during encoding.
source: and reduced lateral prefrontal engagement during encoding (Ghetti et al., 2010; Ghetti and Fandakova, 2020; Shing et al., 2016; Tang et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The availability of mnemonic control strategies may increase with age.
source: suggesting that the availability of mnemonic control strategies may increase with age.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited research on developmental differences in strategic control.

claim: Adaptive memory requires the recruitment and coordination of multiple neural systems, including mechanisms for learning environmental structure, representing value, and engaging strategic control.
source: Taken together, prior work suggests that adaptive memory requires the recruitment and coordination of multiple neural systems, including mechanisms for learning environmental structure, representing value, and engaging strategic control, all of which may undergo marked changes from childhood to adulthood.
evidence: This is a synthesis of prior research findings.

claim: Participants ages 8–25 years (N = 90; 30 children ages 8–12 years; 30 adolescents ages 13–17 years; 30 adults ages 18–25 years) completed two blocks of three tasks while undergoing functional magnetic resonance imaging.
source: Participants ages 8–25 years (N = 90; 30 children ages 8–12 years; 30 adolescents ages 13–17 years; 30 adults ages 18–25 years) completed two blocks of three tasks (Figure 1) while undergoing functional magnetic resonance imaging.
evidence: This describes the study design and sample.

claim: In the frequency-learning task, twelve of the postcards only appeared once, while 12 repeated five times.
source: In the first, frequency-learning task, participants viewed a continuous stream of 24 unique postcards, one at a time. Twelve of the postcards only appeared once, while 12 repeated five times.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the frequency-learning task.

claim: Participants were instructed that in the subsequent task, they would have to stamp all of their postcards, earning one point for each postcard stamped correctly.
source: Participants were instructed that in the subsequent task, they would have to stamp all of their postcards, earning one point for each postcard stamped correctly.
evidence: This describes the task instructions given to participants.

claim: Participants had equal exposure to the to-be-encoded associations across frequency conditions.
source: Critically, in the associative encoding task, regardless of the number of each type of postcard that they had (i.e. 1 or 5), participants saw each type of postcard with its corresponding stamp only once. Thus, participants were informed that the prior frequency of each postcard indicated the value of encoding its associated stamp, but they had equal exposure to the to-be-encoded associations across frequency conditions.
evidence: This describes a key feature of the experimental design.

claim: Frequency of exposure to an item may facilitate subsequent associative memory even when it does not signal the value of information.
source: Because frequency of exposure to an item may facilitate subsequent associative memory even when it does not signal the value of information (Popov and Reder, 2020; Reder et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In a prior behavioral study, frequency only facilitated memory when it signaled the value of remembering information — increased item exposure did not in and of itself enhance subsequent associative memory.
source: in our prior behavioral study (Nussenbaum et al., 2020), we examined the effects of item frequency on subsequent associative memory in two contexts: one in which item frequency signaled information value and one in which it did not. Critically, we found that with our experimental design, frequency only facilitated memory when it signaled the value of remembering information — increased item exposure did not in and of itself enhance subsequent associative memory.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior study by the authors.

claim: Participants across the entire age range demonstrated sensitivity to the frequency of items in their environments.
source: We hypothesized that while participants across our entire age range would demonstrate sensitivity to the frequency of items in their environments, with increasing age, participants would show improvements in transforming this experiential learning into value signals and modulating the engagement of strategic control processes during encoding.
evidence: This was a hypothesis of the study that is later supported by the results.

claim: With increasing age, participants would show improvements in transforming experiential learning into value signals and modulating the engagement of strategic control processes during encoding.
source: We hypothesized that while participants across our entire age range would demonstrate sensitivity to the frequency of items in their environments, with increasing age, participants would show improvements in transforming this experiential learning into value signals and modulating the engagement of strategic control processes during encoding.
evidence: This was a hypothesis of the study that is later supported by the results.

claim: At encoding and retrieval, the recognition of information value would be reflected in increased striatal activation in response to associations involving high- vs. low-frequency items.
source: Neurally, we expected that at encoding and retrieval, the recognition of information value would be reflected in increased striatal activation in response to associations involving high- vs. low-frequency items, while the engagement of strategic control would be reflected in increased activation in lateral prefrontal cortex.
evidence: This was a hypothesis of the study that is later supported by the results.

claim: At encoding and retrieval, the engagement of strategic control would be reflected in increased activation in lateral prefrontal cortex.
source: Neurally, we expected that at encoding and retrieval, the recognition of information value would be reflected in increased striatal activation in response to associations involving high- vs. low-frequency items, while the engagement of strategic control would be reflected in increased activation in lateral prefrontal cortex.
evidence: This was a hypothesis of the study that is later supported by the results.

claim: Increased recruitment of the striatum and prefrontal cortex during encoding and retrieval of high- vs. low-value information would underpin the strengthening of adaptive memory prioritization from childhood to early adulthood.
source: Further, we hypothesized that increased recruitment of the striatum and prefrontal cortex during encoding and retrieval of high- vs. low-value information would underpin the strengthening of adaptive memory prioritization from childhood to early adulthood.
evidence: This was a hypothesis of the study that is later supported by the results.

claim: Participants across the age range responded to new and repeated items with a high degree of accuracy during frequency learning.
source: During frequency learning, participants across our age range responded to new and repeated items with a high degree of accuracy (new items: mean = 0.90, SD = 0.30; repeated items: mean = 0.92, SD = 0.27; Appendix 2—figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from the study.

claim: Older participants demonstrated higher accuracy in correctly identifying both new and repeated items.
source: Older participants demonstrated higher accuracy in correctly identifying both new and repeated items (generalized mixed-effects model results: new items: χ2(1) = 25.52, p < 0.001, repeated items: χ2(1) = 33.43, p < 0.001 Appendix 3—table 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Participants were more accurate in identifying items as 'repeated' as the number of times they saw each item increased.
source: Participants were also more accurate in identifying items as 'repeated' as the number of times they saw each item increased, χ2 = 138.03, p < 0.001, indicating learning throughout the task.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Younger participants demonstrated a larger effect of the number of item repetitions on response accuracy.
source: This effect varied as a function of age — younger participants demonstrated a larger effect of the number of item repetitions on response accuracy, as indicated by a significant interaction, χ2(1) = 17.41, p < 0.001.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Response times to both new and old items decreased with age.
source: Response times to both new and old items decreased with age (Appendix 2—figure 1B, Appendix 3—table 3 and 4; linear mixed-effects model results: new items: F(1, 85.99) = 32.51, p < 0.001; old items: F(1, 87.55) = 21.82, p < 0.001)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Reaction times decreased steeply throughout childhood before leveling off into late adolescence and early adulthood.
source: such that reaction times decreased steeply throughout childhood before leveling off into late adolescence and early adulthood.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of behavioral data showing a nonlinear age effect.

claim: Response times for old items decreased as the number of item repetitions increased.
source: Finally, response times for old items also decreased as the number of item repetitions increased, F(1, 69.94) = 282.21, p < 0.001.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Participants demonstrated greater recruitment of regions of the lateral occipital cortex, the frontal pole, precuneus, angular gyrus, and caudate on the last vs. first appearance of each item.
source: Participants' ability to distinguish old from new items was associated with a wide network of neural regions, some of which demonstrated greater activation in response to the last vs. first appearance of each item, and others of which demonstrated suppressed activation across repetitions. Specifically, whole-brain contrasts revealed greater recruitment of regions of the lateral occipital cortex, the frontal pole, precuneus, angular gyrus, and caudate (among other regions, see Figure 2A and Appendix 4—table 1), on the last vs. first appearance of each item.
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI data and whole-brain analysis.

claim: Participants demonstrated widespread repetition suppression effects, reflected in decreases in neural responsivity in the lateral occipital cortex and temporal occipital cortex on the last vs. first appearance of each item.
source: We observed widespread repetition suppression effects, reflected in decreases in neural responsivity in the lateral occipital cortex and temporal occipital cortex on the last vs. first appearance of each item.
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI data.

claim: Participants demonstrated a robust decrease in activation in the parahippocampal cortex on the last vs. first appearance of each item.
source: In line with our hypothesis, we also observed a robust decrease in activation in the parahippocampal cortex (Figure 2B, Appendix 4—table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI data and is consistent with the study's hypothesis.

claim: Neural activation within the parahippocampal ROI decreased across repetitions.
source: In line with our whole-brain analysis, we observed a main effect of repetition number, F(1, 5015.9) = 30.64, p<0.001, indicating that neural activation within the parahippocampal ROI decreased across repetitions (Appendix 3—table 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by ROI analysis of fMRI data.

claim: The reduction in neural activity in the parahippocampal ROI was greatest across earlier repetitions.
source: Further, we observed a main effect of quadratic repetition number, F(1, 9881.0) = 7.47, p = 0.006, indicating that the reduction in neural activity was greatest across earlier repetitions (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by ROI analysis of fMRI data showing a quadratic effect.

claim: The influence of repetition number on neural activation in the parahippocampal ROI varied with both linear age and quadratic age.
source: Importantly, the influence of repetition number on neural activation varied with both linear age, F(1, 7267.5) = 7.2, p = 0.007, and quadratic age, F(1, 7260.8) = 6.9, p = 0.009.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data.

claim: Repetition suppression was greatest in adulthood, with the steepest increases occurring from late adolescence to early adulthood.
source: These age-related differences suggest that repetition suppression was greatest in adulthood, with the steepest increases occurring from late adolescence to early adulthood (Figure 3).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the age-related differences in repetition suppression observed in the fMRI data.

claim: The decrease in neural activation in the bilateral PHC ROI from the first to fifth repetition of each item increased with both linear age and quadratic age.
source: For each participant for each item, we also computed a 'repetition suppression index' by taking the difference in mean beta values within our ROI on each item's first and last appearance (Ward et al., 2013). These indices demonstrated a similar pattern of age-related variance — we found that the reduction of neural activity from the first to last appearance of the items varied positively with linear age, F(1, 78.32) = 3.97, p = 0.05, and negatively with quadratic age, F(1, 77.55) = 4.8, p = 0.031 (Figure 3B, Appendix 3—table 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of repetition suppression indices derived from fMRI data.

claim: Sensitivity to the repetition of items in the environment was prevalent from childhood to adulthood but increased with age.
source: Taken together, our behavioral and neural results suggest that sensitivity to the repetition of items in the environment was prevalent from childhood to adulthood but increased with age.
evidence: This is a synthesis of behavioral and neural findings.

claim: Error magnitudes in frequency reports decreased with increasing age.
source: We then examined how these report error magnitudes varied as a function of age and frequency condition (Appendix 3—table 7). We observed a main effect of age (F(1, 94.30) = 17.57, p < 0.001) such that error magnitudes decreased with increasing age (Children: Mean = 1.48, SD = 1.34; Adolescents: Mean = 1.10, SD = 1.12; Adults: Mean = 1.13, SD = 1.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Error magnitudes in frequency reports were not related to frequency condition.
source: Error magnitudes were not related to frequency condition (p = 0.993), indicating that participants were not systematically better at representing the 'true' frequencies of items that appeared once or items that appeared five times.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: There was no relation between repetition suppression indices and frequency reports.
source: However, in line with other studies suggesting dissociations between repetition suppression and explicit memory (Ward et al., 2013), we did not observe any relation between repetition suppression indices and frequency reports, F(1, 1360.74) = 0.01, p = 0.903.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no significant relationship.

claim: While parallel developmental improvements were observed in online frequency learning and subsequent explicit reports, they may be driven by separable processes.
source: Thus, while we observed parallel developmental improvements in online frequency learning and subsequent explicit reports, they may be driven by separable processes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lack of correlation between repetition suppression and explicit frequency reports.

claim: Memory accuracy varied as a function of both linear and quadratic age, such that older participants demonstrated higher memory accuracy, with the steepest improvements in memory accuracy occurring from childhood into early adolescence.
source: Memory accuracy varied as a function of both linear (χ2(1) = 8.68, p = 0.003) and quadratic age (χ2(1) = 4.24, p = 0.039), such that older participants demonstrated higher memory accuracy, with the steepest improvements in memory accuracy occurring from childhood into early adolescence (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of memory performance data.

claim: Individuals used naturalistic value signals to prioritize memory for high-value information.
source: In line with our hypothesis, we observed a main effect of frequency condition on memory, χ2(1) = 19.73, p < 0.001, indicating that individuals used naturalistic value signals to prioritize memory for high-value information.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of memory performance data.

claim: The influence of frequency condition on memory increased to the greatest extent throughout childhood and early adolescence.
source: Critically, this effect interacted with both linear age (χ2(1) = 10.74, p = 0.001) and quadratic age (χ2(1) = 9.27, p = 0.002), such that the influence of frequency condition on memory increased to the greatest extent throughout childhood and early adolescence.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing age interactions with frequency condition.

claim: The influence of frequency condition on memory significantly increased from age 8 to age 15.86.
source: The results of this analysis revealed that the influence of frequency condition on memory significantly increased from age 8 to age 15.86 (b = 0.03, z = 2.71, p = 0.0068; Appendix 2—figure 2)
evidence: This claim is supported by a two-lines test analysis of the data.

claim: The influence of frequency condition on memory only marginally decreased from age 15.86 to age 25.
source: but only marginally decreased from age 15.86 to age 25 (b = −0.02, z = 1.91, p = 0.0576).
evidence: This claim is supported by a two-lines test analysis of the data.

claim: Explicit frequency report error magnitude predicted overall memory performance.
source: Here, explicit frequency report error magnitude predicted overall memory performance, χ2(1) = 13.05, p < 0.001
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis including frequency report error as a covariate.

claim: When controlling for frequency learning measures, age differences in initial learning did not account for age differences in the use of environmental regularities to strategically prioritize memory for valuable information.
source: Thus, while age differences in initial learning related to overall memory performance, they did not account for age differences in the use of environmental regularities to strategically prioritize memory for valuable information.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from statistical models that controlled for frequency learning measures.

claim: Participants demonstrated increased engagement of the left lateral PFC and bilateral caudate during encoding of the pairs involving high-frequency items relative to pairs involving low-frequency items.
source: In line with our hypothesis, a whole-brain contrast revealed increased engagement of the left lateral PFC and bilateral caudate (1765 voxels at x = −51, y = 42, z = 9; 232 voxels at x = 18, y = 12, z = 6; and 54 voxels at x = 18, y = 18, and z = 12; Figure 5A, Appendix 4—table 4) during encoding of the pairs involving high-frequency items relative to pairs involving low-frequency items.
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-brain fMRI analysis.

claim: Participants who demonstrated the greatest difference in memory accuracy for pairs involving high-frequency vs. low-frequency items also demonstrated greater value-based modulation of left lateral PFC activation.
source: Participants who demonstrated the greatest difference in memory accuracy for pairs involving high-frequency vs. low-frequency items also demonstrated greater value-based modulation of left lateral PFC activation (232 voxels at x = −48, y = 21, z = 27; Figure 5B, Appendix 4—table 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI analysis including memory difference scores as a covariate.

claim: When restricting analysis to associations that were subsequently retrieved correctly, participants demonstrated increased recruitment of the left lateral prefrontal cortex and left caudate during encoding of high- vs. low- value pairs.
source: To de-confound the effects of value vs. subsequent memory accuracy on neural activation at encoding, we re-ran our high- vs. low-value contrast but restricted our analysis to associations that were subsequently retrieved correctly. We observed similar neural effects — increased recruitment of the left lateral prefrontal cortex and left caudate during encoding of high- vs. low- value pairs (1042 voxels at x = −42, y = 15, z = 30; 124 voxels at x = −12, y = −3, z = 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI analysis restricted to correctly remembered items.

claim: Successful encoding was associated with increased activation in left lateral PFC but not differential recruitment of the caudate.
source: Further, neural signatures of successful vs. unsuccessful encoding differed from those of high- vs. low-value encoding. Though we observed similar activation in left lateral PFC (1273 voxels at x = −48, y = 9, z = 27; Appendix 4—table 6), here, we did not observe differential recruitment of the caudate.
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI analysis comparing successful vs. unsuccessful encoding.

claim: Successful encoding was associated with increased activation in the right hippocampus.
source: In addition, consistent with previous observations of subsequent memory effects (Davachi, 2006), successful encoding was associated with increased activation in the right hippocampus (21 voxels at x = 24, y = −6, z = −21).
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI analysis and is consistent with prior research.

claim: During encoding, older participants demonstrated greater recruitment of the left lateral PFC and the right lateral PFC.
source: Across trial types, during encoding, we observed widespread age-related increases in neural activation (Appendix 4—table 3), in regions including the left lateral PFC (120 voxels at x = −54, y = 12, z = 33) and the right lateral PFC (24 voxels at x = 48, y = 12, z = 30; Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI analysis examining age-related differences in neural activation.

claim: Caudate activation during encoding of high- vs. low-value associations did not vary significantly as a function of age.
source: Caudate activation did not vary significantly as a function of age (β = 0.16, SE = 0.11, p = 0.126) (Appendix 3—table 12), indicating that participants across our age range demonstrated similarly increased recruitment of the caudate while encoding high- vs. low-value associations.
evidence: This claim is supported by ROI analysis of fMRI data.

claim: PFC activation during encoding of high- vs. low-value associations varied as a function of both linear and quadratic age, such that the difference in PFC engagement increased to the greatest extent throughout childhood and early adolescence.
source: PFC activation, however, demonstrated a different pattern, varying as a function of both linear (β = 1.97, SE = 0.74, p = 0.01) and quadratic age (β = −1.73, SE = 0.73, p = 0.021), such that the difference in PFC engagement during encoding of high- vs. low-value associations increased to the greatest extent throughout childhood and early adolescence (Appendix 2—figure 3, Appendix 3—table 13).
evidence: This claim is supported by ROI analysis of fMRI data.

claim: PFC modulation predicted memory difference scores, even when controlling for age.
source: First, we confirmed that in line with our whole-brain analysis, PFC modulation predicted memory difference scores, even when controlling for age (β = 0.34, SE = 0.10, p = 0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Memory difference scores varied with age, with older participants demonstrating a larger difference in memory accuracy for high- vs. low- value associations.
source: Next, we confirmed that these difference scores did in fact vary with age (β = 0.22, SE = 0.10, p = 0.041), with older participants demonstrating a larger difference in memory accuracy for high- vs. low- value associations.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: When controlling for PFC activation, age no longer related to memory difference scores.
source: Critically, however, when controlling for PFC activation, age no longer related to memory difference scores (β = 0.15, SE = 0.10, p = 0.14).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: PFC activation fully mediated the relation between linear age and memory difference scores.
source: A formal mediation analysis revealed that PFC activation fully mediated the relation between linear age and memory difference scores (standardized indirect effect: .07, 95% confidence interval: [.01, .15], p = 0.017; standardized direct effect: .15, 95% confidence interval: [−0.03, .33], p = 0.108; Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by mediation analysis.

claim: Age did not mediate the relation between PFC activation and memory difference scores.
source: This relation was directionally specific; age did not mediate the relation between PFC activation and memory difference scores (standardized indirect effect: .03, 95% confidence interval: [−0.007, .09], p = 0.13; standardized direct effect: .34, 95% confidence interval: [.14, .54], p < 0.001.)
evidence: This claim is supported by mediation analysis.

claim: When including quadratic age, WASI scores, online frequency learning accuracy, and mean explicit frequency report error magnitudes as control variables, PFC activation continued to mediate the relation between linear age and memory difference scores.
source: Further, when we included quadratic age, WASI scores, online frequency learning accuracy, online frequency learning accuracy on the final repetition of each item, and mean explicit frequency report error magnitudes as control variables in the mediation analysis, PFC activation continued to mediate the relation between linear age and memory difference scores (standardized indirect effect: .56, 95% confidence interval: [0.06, 1.35], p = 0.023; standardized direct effect: 1.75, 95% confidence interval: [0.12, 3.38], p = 0.034).
evidence: This claim is supported by mediation analysis with additional control variables.

claim: During retrieval, older participants demonstrated greater recruitment of bilateral PFC.
source: As during encoding, a whole-brain contrast comparing retrieval trials to baseline revealed age-related differences in bilateral PFC recruitment (Figure 7A; 42 voxels at x = 51, y = 3, z = 21; 36 voxels at x = −60, y = 6, z = 21) as well as regions of occipital cortex (see Appendix 4—table 7) across trials during retrieval.
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-brain fMRI analysis.

claim: During retrieval of associations involving high- vs. low-frequency items, participants demonstrated increased engagement of the left lateral PFC and the bilateral caudate.
source: During retrieval of associations involving high- vs. low-frequency items, we continued to observe increased engagement of the left lateral PFC (Figure 7B; 116 voxels at x = −48, y = 21, z = 24) and the bilateral caudate (128 voxels at x = −12, y = −6, z = 15 and 77 voxels at x = 15, y = −3, z = 21).
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-brain fMRI analysis.

claim: Neural activation during retrieval of high- vs. low-value associations was not related to age or memory difference scores.
source: This activation was not related to age or memory difference scores.
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI analysis.

claim: Participants demonstrated better associative memory for pairs involving items they reported were more frequent.
source: Participants demonstrated better associative memory for pairs involving items they reported were more frequent, χ2(1) = 31.20, p < 0.001 (Figure 8A).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: The effect of explicit frequency reports on memory was modulated by age and quadratic age, indicating that participants' beliefs about item frequency influenced memory to the greatest degree in adolescence and early adulthood.
source: This effect was modulated by age (χ2(1) = 10.37, p = 0.001) and quadratic age (χ2(1) = 9.50, p = 0.002), indicating that participants' beliefs about item frequency influenced memory to the greatest degree in adolescence and early adulthood.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing age interactions.

claim: The linear model including explicit frequency reports fit the data better than the linear model including the true frequency condition.
source: Further, replicating our previous behavioral findings (Nussenbaum et al., 2020), we found that the linear model including explicit frequency reports (BIC = 5438.37) fit the data better than the linear model including the true frequency condition (BIC = 5449.19, χ2 = 10.83, p < 0.001), indicating that participants' representations of item frequency influenced memory to a greater extent than the true item frequencies.
evidence: This claim is supported by model comparison analysis.

claim: Repetition suppression during frequency learning predicted subsequent associative memory for high-frequency items.
source: We found that repetition suppression during frequency learning did indeed predict subsequent associative memory, χ2(1) = 11.21, p < 0.001 (Figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis relating neural and behavioral measures.

claim: The effect of repetition suppression on memory did not interact with age.
source: This effect did not interact with age, χ2(1) = 0.79, p = 0.374.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: When both repetition suppression indices and explicit frequency reports were included in the model, both predictors continued to explain significant variance in memory accuracy.
source: Further, when we included both repetition suppression indices and explicit frequency reports in our model, both predictors continued to explain significant variance in memory accuracy (Frequency reports: χ2(1) = 21.16, p < 0.001, Repetition suppression: χ2(1) = 10.25, p = 0.001), suggesting that learned value signals that guide memory may be derived from multiple, distinct representations of prior experience.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis including both predictors.

claim: Learned value signals that guide memory may be derived from multiple, distinct representations of prior experience.
source: suggesting that learned value signals that guide memory may be derived from multiple, distinct representations of prior experience.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the finding that both repetition suppression and explicit frequency reports independently predict memory.

claim: Participants with greater frequency distances demonstrated greater PFC activation during encoding of pairs with high- vs. low-frequency items.
source: We did, however, observe a significant effect of frequency distance on PFC activation (β = 0.42, SE = 0.12, p = 0.0012), such that participants who believed that average frequencies of the high- and low-frequency items were further apart also demonstrated greater PFC activation during encoding of pairs with high- vs. low-frequency items (Appendix 3—tables 21 and 22).
evidence: This claim is supported by regression analysis relating behavioral and neural measures.

claim: When accounting for both PFC activation and frequency distances, there continued to be an effect of age on memory difference scores.
source: Importantly, however, even when we accounted for both PFC activation and frequency distances, we continued to observe an effect of age on memory difference scores (β = 0.56, SE = 0.20, p = 0.006) (Appendix 3—table 23)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis including multiple predictors.

claim: Developmental differences in value-guided memory are not driven solely by age differences in beliefs about the structure of the environment but also depend on the use of those beliefs to guide encoding.
source: which, together with our prior analyses (Appendix 3—table 16), suggest that developmental differences in value-guided memory are not driven solely by age differences in beliefs about the structure of the environment but also depend on the use of those beliefs to guide encoding.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple statistical analyses.

claim: During encoding and retrieval, high- relative to low-value stimuli elicited increased activation in regions sensitive to value and motivational salience, including the caudate, and those associated with strategic control processes, including the lateral PFC.
source: In line with studies of motivated memory in adults (Cohen et al., 2014), we found that during encoding and retrieval, high- relative to low-value stimuli elicited increased activation in regions sensitive to value and motivational salience, including the caudate (Delgado et al., 2004), and those associated with strategic control processes, including the lateral PFC (Badre and Wagner, 2007; Cole and Schneider, 2007; Power and Petersen, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by the study's fMRI data and is consistent with prior research.

claim: Value-guided memory selectivity improved across childhood and adolescence.
source: Further, replicating previous work, we found that value-guided memory selectivity improved across childhood and adolescence (Castel et al., 2011; Hanten et al., 2007; Nussenbaum et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by the study's behavioral data and replicates prior research.

claim: Increased engagement of the lateral PFC during encoding mediated the relation between age and memory selectivity.
source: Critically, here we demonstrate that increased engagement of the lateral PFC during encoding mediated the relation between age and memory selectivity.
evidence: This claim is supported by mediation analysis of the study's data.

claim: The relation between PFC activation and memory selectivity was specific to the lateral PFC — although the caudate similarly demonstrated increased activation during encoding of high- vs. low-value information, value-based modulation of caudate activation did not vary as a function of age and did not relate to memory selectivity.
source: This relation was specific to the lateral PFC — although the caudate similarly demonstrated increased activation during encoding of high- vs. low-value information, value-based modulation of caudate activation did not vary as a function of age and did not relate to memory selectivity.
evidence: This claim is supported by the study's fMRI data showing differential age effects for PFC vs. caudate.

claim: All participants demonstrated a similar relation between repetition suppression and subsequent associative memory.
source: While all participants demonstrated a similar relation between repetition suppression and subsequent associative memory, the association between explicit frequency reports and memory was greater in older participants.
evidence: This claim is supported by the study's analysis showing no age interaction for repetition suppression effects on memory.

claim: The association between explicit frequency reports and memory was greater in older participants.
source: While all participants demonstrated a similar relation between repetition suppression and subsequent associative memory, the association between explicit frequency reports and memory was greater in older participants.
evidence: This claim is supported by the study's analysis showing an age interaction for explicit frequency report effects on memory.

claim: The divergent developmental trajectories of repetition suppression and explicit frequency report effects on memory suggest that the influence of learned value on memory arises through distinct cognitive processes.
source: These divergent developmental trajectories suggest that the influence of learned value on memory arises through distinct cognitive processes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the different age-related patterns observed for the two types of learning signals.

claim: Explicit beliefs about information value may have triggered the engagement of strategic control.
source: One possibility is that while explicit beliefs about information value triggered the engagement of strategic control, stimulus familiarity (as indexed by repetition suppression [Gonsalves et al., 2005]) may have facilitated encoding of novel associations, even in the absence of controlled strategy use.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Stimulus familiarity may have facilitated encoding of novel associations, even in the absence of controlled strategy use.
source: One possibility is that while explicit beliefs about information value triggered the engagement of strategic control, stimulus familiarity (as indexed by repetition suppression [Gonsalves et al., 2005]) may have facilitated encoding of novel associations, even in the absence of controlled strategy use.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Prior work suggests that stronger memory traces for constituent components enhance associative memory.
source: Indeed, prior work suggests that stronger memory traces for constituent components enhance associative memory (Chalmers and Humphreys, 2003; Popov and Reder, 2020; Reder et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In a prior behavioral study, removing the relation between item frequency and reward value eliminated the memory benefit for associations involving high-frequency items.
source: However, in our previous behavioral work (Nussenbaum et al., 2020), we found that removing the relation between item frequency and reward value eliminated the memory benefit for associations involving high-frequency items, suggesting that stimulus familiarity itself did not account for the influence of item frequency on memory in our task.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior study by the authors.

claim: When frequency predicts value, stimulus familiarity may serve as a proxy for information utility.
source: Still, when frequency does predict value, stimulus familiarity may serve as a proxy for information utility.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of how familiarity might influence memory in the current task.

claim: Familiarity signals may exert age-invariant effects on subsequent memory, whereas explicit beliefs about item frequency may more strongly facilitate subsequent memory with increasing age.
source: This familiarity signal may exert age-invariant effects on subsequent memory, whereas explicit beliefs about item frequency may more strongly facilitate subsequent memory with increasing age.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the age-related differences observed in the study.

claim: Age differences in learning cannot fully account for age differences in value-guided memory.
source: Importantly, although we observed age-related differences in participants' learning of the structure of their environments, the strengthening of the relation between frequency reports and associative memory with increasing age suggests that age differences in learning cannot fully account for age differences in value-guided memory.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's analyses.

claim: Even when accounting for individual differences in participants' explicit knowledge of the structure of the environment, older participants demonstrated a stronger relation between their beliefs about item frequency and associative memory.
source: Even when accounting for individual differences in participants' explicit knowledge of the structure of the environment, older participants demonstrated a stronger relation between their beliefs about item frequency and associative memory, suggesting that they used their beliefs to guide memory to a greater degree than younger participants.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analyses controlling for frequency knowledge.

claim: Older participants used their beliefs about item frequency to guide memory to a greater degree than younger participants.
source: suggesting that they used their beliefs to guide memory to a greater degree than younger participants.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the age-related differences in the relationship between frequency beliefs and memory.

claim: The interaction between age and frequency condition on associative memory remained robust even when controlling for age-related differences in the accuracy of both online frequency learning and explicit frequency reports.
source: In addition, we continued to observe a robust interaction between age and frequency condition on associative memory, even when controlling for age-related differences in the accuracy of both online frequency learning and explicit frequency reports.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analyses including control variables.

claim: Developmental differences in memory were driven by both knowledge of the structure of the environment and use of that knowledge to guide encoding.
source: Our neural results further suggest that developmental differences in memory were driven by both knowledge of the structure of the environment and use of that knowledge to guide encoding.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's neural and behavioral findings.

claim: Age-related increases in both overall PFC engagement as well as its value-based modulation may reflect developmental differences in the engagement of strategic control.
source: Specifically, we observed age-related increases in both overall PFC engagement as well as its value-based modulation, which may reflect developmental differences in the engagement of strategic control.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the neural findings.

claim: The finding that lateral prefrontal cortex activation during encoding of high- vs. low-value information may underpin memory selectivity is in line with prior studies of motivated memory in older adults.
source: Our finding that lateral prefrontal cortex activation during encoding of high- vs. low-value information may underpin memory selectivity is also in line with prior studies of motivated memory in older adults (Cohen et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim relates the current findings to prior research in older adults.

claim: Older adults demonstrate decreased neural activation in response to value cues but preserved memory selectivity.
source: Older adults have been shown to demonstrate decreased neural activation in response to value cues (Cohen et al., 2016; Geddes et al., 2018) but preserved memory selectivity (Castel, 2007; Castel et al., 2002; Cohen et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In older adults, memory selectivity is supported by the strategic recruitment of the left lateral PFC during encoding of high- vs. low-value information.
source: supported by the strategic recruitment of the left lateral PFC during encoding of high- vs. low-value information (Cohen et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The PFC may support enhanced attention and semantic elaboration during encoding.
source: The PFC may support enhanced attention (Uncapher et al., 2011; Uncapher and Wagner, 2009) and semantic elaboration (Kirchhoff and Buckner, 2006) during encoding
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The PFC may support more focused and organized search and selection during retrieval.
source: and more focused (Wais et al., 2012) and organized search and selection (Badre and Wagner, 2007; Yu et al., 2018) during retrieval.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: From childhood to young adulthood, individuals demonstrate improvements in the implementation of strategic memory processes.
source: From childhood to young adulthood, individuals demonstrate improvements in the implementation of strategic memory processes (Bjorkland et al., 2009; Yu et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Improvements in strategic memory processes are paralleled by increases in PFC recruitment during both encoding and retrieval.
source: which are paralleled by increases in PFC recruitment during both encoding and retrieval (Ghetti et al., 2010; Ghetti and Fandakova, 2020; Ofen et al., 2007; Shing et al., 2016; Tang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The current study observed age-related improvements in overall memory performance and in prefrontal recruitment during encoding and retrieval of novel associations, in line with prior work.
source: In line with this prior work, we similarly observed age-related improvements in overall memory performance and in prefrontal recruitment during encoding and retrieval of novel associations.
evidence: This claim is supported by the study's data and relates it to prior research.

claim: The development of adaptive memory requires not only the implementation of encoding and retrieval strategies, but also the flexibility to up- or down-regulate the engagement of control in response to momentary fluctuations in information value.
source: The development of adaptive memory requires not only the implementation of encoding and retrieval strategies, but also the flexibility to up- or down-regulate the engagement of control in response to momentary fluctuations in information value (Castel et al., 2007; Castel et al., 2013; Hennessee et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Value-based modulation of lateral PFC engagement during encoding mediated the relation between age and memory selectivity, suggesting that developmental change in both the representation of learned value and value-guided cognitive control may underpin the emergence of adaptive memory prioritization.
source: Importantly, value-based modulation of lateral PFC engagement during encoding mediated the relation between age and memory selectivity, suggesting that developmental change in both the representation of learned value and value-guided cognitive control may underpin the emergence of adaptive memory prioritization.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mediation analysis.

claim: Prior work examining other neurocognitive processes has found that increases in the flexible upregulation of control in response to value cues enhance goal-directed behavior across development.
source: Prior work examining other neurocognitive processes, including response inhibition (Insel et al., 2017) and selective attention (Störmer et al., 2014), has similarly found that increases in the flexible upregulation of control in response to value cues enhance goal-directed behavior across development (Davidow et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The flexible upregulation of control in response to value cues may depend on the engagement of both striatal and prefrontal circuitry.
source: and may depend on the engagement of both striatal and prefrontal circuitry (Hallquist et al., 2018; Insel et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The current study extends past findings to the domain of memory, demonstrating that value signals derived from the structure of the environment increasingly elicit prefrontal cortex engagement and strengthen goal-directed encoding across childhood and into adolescence.
source: Here, we extend these past findings to the domain of memory, demonstrating that value signals derived from the structure of the environment increasingly elicit prefrontal cortex engagement and strengthen goal-directed encoding across childhood and into adolescence.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's contribution relative to prior work.

claim: In the absence of explicit value cues, the engagement of prefrontal control processes may reflect beliefs about information value that are learned through experience.
source: Further, we also demonstrate that in the absence of explicit value cues, the engagement of prefrontal control processes may reflect beliefs about information value that are learned through experience.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Participants who represented the average frequencies of the low- and high-frequency items as further apart demonstrated greater value-based modulation of lateral PFC activation.
source: Here, we found that differential PFC activation during encoding of high- vs. low-value information reflected individual and age-related differences in beliefs about the structure of the environment; participants who represented the average frequencies of the low- and high-frequency items as further apart also demonstrated greater value-based modulation of lateral PFC activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by regression analysis of the study's data.

claim: Explicit frequency reports were collected after associative encoding and retrieval.
source: It is important to note, however, that we collected explicit frequency reports after associative encoding and retrieval.
evidence: This describes the timing of data collection in the study.

claim: The relation between PFC activation and explicit frequency reports may be bidirectional.
source: Thus, the relation between PFC activation and explicit frequency reports may be bidirectional — while participants may have increased the recruitment of cognitive control processes to better encode information they believed was more valuable, the engagement of more elaborative or deeper encoding strategies that led to stronger memory traces may have also increased participants' subjective sense of an item's frequency (Jonides and Naveh-Benjamin, 1987).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation acknowledging the limitations of the study design.

claim: During retrieval, increased activation of the caudate and dlPFC for high- vs. low-value pairs did not significantly vary as a function of memory difference scores or age.
source: During retrieval, we continued to observe increased activation of the caudate and dlPFC for high- vs. low-value pairs. However, this activation did not significantly vary as a function of memory difference scores or age
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI analysis during retrieval.

claim: The developmental differences in value-guided memory observed in the study were likely driven by age-related change in encoding processes.
source: suggesting that the developmental differences in value-guided memory that we observed were likely driven by age-related change in encoding processes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lack of age effects during retrieval.

claim: Memory prioritization varied with quadratic age in the current study.
source: We found that memory prioritization varied with quadratic age, and our follow-up tests probing the quadratic age effect did not reveal evidence for significant age-related change in memory prioritization between late adolescence and early adulthood.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the study's data.

claim: In a prior behavioral study using a very similar paradigm, memory prioritization varied with linear age only.
source: However, in our prior behavioral work using a very similar paradigm (Nussenbaum et al., 2020), we found that memory prioritization varied with linear age only.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior study by the authors.

claim: Subtle differences in the control demands between tasks may shift the age range across which differences in behavior are observed.
source: In line with theoretical proposals (Davidow et al., 2018), subtle differences in the control demands between the two tasks (e.g. reducing the number of 'foils' presented on each trial of the memory test here relative to our prior study), may have shifted the age range across which we observed differences in behavior, with the more demanding variant of our task showing more linear age-related improvements into early adulthood.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of differences between the current and prior study.

claim: The specific control demands of the task may have influenced the age at which value-guided memory emerged.
source: In addition, the specific control demands of our task may have also influenced the age at which value-guided memory emerged.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Future studies should test whether younger children can modulate encoding based on the value of information if the mnemonic demands of the task are simpler.
source: Future studies should test whether younger children can modulate encoding based on the value of information if the mnemonic demands of the task are simpler.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research.

claim: The study was cross-sectional.
source: One important caveat is that our study was cross-sectional
evidence: This describes the study design.

claim: It will be important to replicate the findings in a longitudinal sample to measure more directly how developmental changes in cognitive control within an individual contribute to changes in their ability to selectively encode useful information.
source: it will be important to replicate our findings in a longitudinal sample to measure more directly how developmental changes in cognitive control within an individual contribute to changes in their ability to selectively encode useful information.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research to address limitations of the current study.

claim: In cross-sectional samples, variables can emerge as significant mediators of age-related change due largely to statistical artifact.
source: Our mediation results, in particular, must be interpreted with caution, as simulations have demonstrated that in cross-sectional samples, variables can emerge as significant mediators of age-related change due largely to statistical artifact (Hofer et al., 2006; Lindenberger et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior methodological research.

claim: The finding that PFC activation mediates the relation between age and value-guided memory does not necessarily imply that within an individual, PFC development leads to improvements in memory selectivity.
source: Indeed, our finding that PFC activation mediates the relation between age and value-guided memory does not necessarily imply that within an individual, PFC development leads to improvements in memory selectivity.
evidence: This is a cautionary statement about interpreting cross-sectional mediation results.

claim: Longitudinal work in which individuals' neural activity and memory performance is sampled densely within developmental windows of interest is needed to elucidate the complex relations between age, brain development, and behavior.
source: Longitudinal work in which individuals' neural activity and memory performance is sampled densely within developmental windows of interest is needed to elucidate the complex relations between age, brain development, and behavior (Hofer et al., 2006; Lindenberger et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research supported by citations to methodological literature.

claim: The study did not find evidence to support the hypothesis that both the ventral and dorsal striatum may be involved in encoding of high-value information.
source: We did not find evidence to support two of our predictions. First, although we initially hypothesized that both the ventral and dorsal striatum may be involved in encoding of high-value information, the activation we observed was largely within the dorsal striatum
evidence: This describes a finding that did not support the initial hypothesis.

claim: The dorsal striatum is a region that may reflect the value of goal-directed actions.
source: a region that may reflect the value of goal-directed actions (Liljeholm and O'Doherty, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Rather than each stimulus acquiring intrinsic value during frequency learning, participants may have represented the value of the 'action' of remembering each pair during encoding.
source: In our task, rather than each stimulus acquiring intrinsic value during frequency learning, participants may have represented the value of the 'action' of remembering each pair during encoding.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the dorsal striatum activation.

claim: The study did not observe differences in hippocampal engagement during encoding or retrieval of high- vs. low-value associates.
source: Second, we did not observe differences in hippocampal engagement during encoding or retrieval of high- vs. low-value associates.
evidence: This describes a finding that did not support the initial hypothesis.

claim: Prior work has suggested that value cues bolster memory through their influence on medial temporal lobe activity.
source: This is somewhat surprising, as prior work has suggested that value cues bolster memory through their influence on medial temporal lobe activity (Adcock et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Because the task required the use of learned value signals, memory retrieval processes may have been required on every encoding trial to recall the frequency of each item.
source: However, because our task required the use of learned value signals, memory retrieval processes may have been required on every encoding trial to recall the frequency of each item.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of why hippocampal differences were not observed.

claim: All items presented at encoding may have triggered the engagement of hippocampal-dependent retrieval processes that underpin many forms of memory-guided behavior including attention and decision-making.
source: Thus, all items presented at encoding may have triggered the engagement of hippocampal-dependent retrieval processes (Squire, 1992) that underpin many forms of memory-guided behavior including attention (Stokes et al., 2012; Summerfield et al., 2006) and decision-making (Murty et al., 2016; Shadlen and Shohamy, 2016; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The study observed increased activation in the hippocampus during encoding of associations that were subsequently remembered vs. those that were subsequently forgotten, in line with prior work.
source: Further, in line with prior work (Davachi, 2006), we did observe increased activation in the hippocampus during encoding of associations that were subsequently remembered vs. those that were subsequently forgotten.
evidence: This claim is supported by the study's data and is consistent with prior research.

claim: Medial temporal activation, including hippocampal activation, may more strongly reflect successful memory formation — whether or not it was facilitated by value — whereas the caudate and lateral prefrontal cortex may be more sensitive to fluctuations in the engagement of value-guided cognitive control.
source: Medial temporal activation, including hippocampal activation, may thus more strongly reflect successful memory formation — whether or not it was facilitated by value — whereas the caudate and lateral prefrontal cortex may be more sensitive to fluctuations in the engagement of value-guided cognitive control.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the different patterns of activation observed across brain regions.

claim: There are multiple routes through which value signals influence memory.
source: There are multiple routes through which value signals influence memory (Cohen et al., 2019b)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: In many contexts, reward-motivated memory may not require strategic control.
source: and in many contexts, reward-motivated memory may not require strategic control.
evidence: This is a general statement about memory processes.

claim: Value anticipation and reward delivery lead to dopaminergic release in the VTA, which projects to corticostriatal circuits and directly to the hippocampus and medial temporal lobes.
source: Value anticipation and reward delivery lead to dopaminergic release in the VTA, which projects not only to corticostriatal circuits that implement goal-directed strategy selection (Liljeholm and O'Doherty, 2012), but also directly to the hippocampus and medial temporal lobes (Adcock et al., 2006; Lisman and Grace, 2005; Murty et al., 2017; Shohamy and Adcock, 2010; Stanek et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Given the earlier development of subcortically restricted circuitry relative to the more protracted development of cortical-subcortical pathways, the direct influence of reward on memory may develop earlier than the controlled pathway studied in the current research.
source: Given the earlier development of subcortically restricted circuitry relative to the more protracted development of cortical-subcortical pathways (Somerville and Casey, 2010), it may be the case that the direct influence of reward on memory develops earlier than the controlled pathway we studied here.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on prior knowledge of brain development.

claim: A pathway involving direct dopaminergic influence on the hippocampus can be engaged through direct delivery of rewards or reinforcement signals at the time of encoding.
source: Rather than eliciting strategic control through incentivizing successful memory, this pathway can be engaged through direct delivery of rewards or reinforcement signals at the time of encoding (Ergo et al., 2020; Jang et al., 2019; Rosenbaum et al., 2020; Rouhani et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In one study, adolescents demonstrated greater reward-based modulation of hippocampal-striatal connectivity than adults, and the strength of this connectivity predicted reward-related memory.
source: In one such study, adolescents demonstrated greater reward-based modulation of hippocampal-striatal connectivity than adults, and the strength of this connectivity predicted reward-related memory (Davidow et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Other studies have not found evidence for developmental change in the influence of valenced outcomes on memory.
source: However, other studies have not found evidence for developmental change in the influence of valenced outcomes on memory (Cohen et al., 2019a; Katzman and Hartley, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The influence of different motivational and reward signals on memory across development may not be straightforward.
source: The influence of different motivational and reward signals on memory across development may not be straightforward
evidence: This is a general statement about the complexity of developmental effects.

claim: Individual and developmental differences in neurocognitive processes including sensitivity to valenced feedback, curiosity, and emotional processing may interact, leading to complex relations between age, motivation, and memory performance.
source: individual and developmental differences in neurocognitive processes including sensitivity to valenced feedback (Ngo et al., 2019; Rosenbaum et al., 2020), curiosity (Fandakova and Gruber, 2021), and emotional processing (Adelman and Estes, 2013; Eich and Castel, 2016) may interact, leading to complex relations between age, motivation, and memory performance.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Further work is needed to characterize both the influence of different types of reward signals on memory across development, as well as the development of the neural pathways that underlie age-related change in behavior.
source: Further work is needed to characterize both the influence of different types of reward signals on memory across development, as well as the development of the neural pathways that underlie age-related change in behavior.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research.

claim: The present study contributes to our understanding of the neurocognitive mechanisms that support memory across development.
source: The present study contributes to our understanding of the neurocognitive mechanisms that support memory across development.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the study's contribution.

claim: The study addressed the question of how motivated memory may operate in the absence of explicit value cues by examining the development of the neurocognitive mechanisms that support the learning and use of information value to guide encoding and retrieval.
source: Specifically, we addressed the question of how motivated memory may operate in the absence of explicit value cues by examining the development of the neurocognitive mechanisms that support the learning and use of information value to guide encoding and retrieval.
evidence: This describes the study's research question.

claim: The findings suggest that while development is marked by improvements in the ability to learn about the statistical structure of the environment, the emergence of adaptive memory also depends centrally on age-related differences in prefrontal control.
source: The present findings suggest that while development is marked by improvements in the ability to learn about the statistical structure of the environment, the emergence of adaptive memory also depends centrally on age-related differences in prefrontal control.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's main findings.

claim: The findings demonstrate that prefrontal cortex development has implications not just for general memory processes but for the selective prioritization of useful information — a key component of adaptive memory throughout the lifespan.
source: Our findings demonstrate that prefrontal cortex development has implications not just for general memory processes but for the selective prioritization of useful information — a key component of adaptive memory throughout the lifespan.
